posts.text:
What did we just see with Riemann and what does it mean?  And why isn‘t it immediately rescuing the market?

A meditation on how many here are misunderstanding both the nature of and the implications of the Riemann results.

A key fact about the brilliant Riemann results that many people here are missing: AI *alone* did not solve the Reimann hypothesis. 

Instead an exceptionally talented mathematician with expertise in AI worked together with AI to jointly solve RH.  

As AI math pioneer @ChrSzegedy put, it “Levent made all the right (life) choices at the right time” in order to achieve the result, and we wouldn’t be here others. He didn’t just type in a prompt “Solve Riemann” and get the answer.

Fundamentally, rather, a brilliant mathematician with brilliant instanct drove the process. It took months and a lot of iteration.

And he relied on a special set of resources (see below) that you won’t did for example in medicine.

What actually happened is still super impressive — but it is not what thousands of people seem to believe, and it doesn’t have the same implications.

It does not mean for example that AGI has arrived, or anything like that. (If it had, you wouldn’t have needed the human mathematician to guide the whole process.) 

The other thing that a lot of people aren’t getting is that the RH solution depended on a special-purpose symbolic AI solver with 16 millions of lines of code - built over multiple years by perhaps hundreds  of people — for a specific purpose that is of relatively little value for solving more open-end problems in domains like biology, business, or robotics.  (As I predicted in 2024, verifiable methods have help more with math than other domains.)

Or as @jeremyakahn just put it “Solving RH doesn’t help you negotiate a contract better or correctly figure out a corporate tax return. So no real change to enterprise value prop.”  As @sebkrier put, “Solving an old pure math problem does not immediately widen Anthropic's operating margins"

It’s kind of like what we saw when DeepBlue beat @Kasparov63 in chess in 1997; an absolutely amazing use of brute force in a special-purpose way that didn’t generalize to all that much else. 

The market seems to get all of this - RH hasn’t moved $ANT much after hours – even if a lot of people here don’t.

Paraphrasing something I said here yesterday, clinging to the Riemann results like a life raft after the stock market correction doesn’t change the fact that (a) current AI still isn’t trustworthy enough to for many applications and (b) is still not profitable enough to warrant the massive investments.

In 2006, Apple asked Intel to build the chip for the first iPhone.

Intel said no.

At the time, Intel was worth $116.8 billion.

Apple was already putting Intel chips inside Mac computers.
So Steve Jobs went to Intel CEO Paul Otellini first.

Apple set a strict ceiling price and wouldn't budge.
It would pay "not a nickel more" per chip.

Intel's team ran the cost numbers.
The price looked too low, and Intel didn't think the phone would sell in big numbers.

So Intel walked away.

In June 2006, Intel went further.
It sold its mobile chip unit, XScale, to Marvell Technology for $600 million.

Apple turned to ARM architecture instead.
Samsung built the early iPhone chips.

In May 2013, Otellini retired and told The Atlantic what went wrong.
He said "the forecasted cost was wrong and the volume was 100x what anyone thought."

He added: "My gut told me to say yes."

In September 2014, Apple moved its flagship A8 iPhone chip orders to TSMC on its 20nm line.

iPhone volume fueled TSMC's rise in advanced chipmaking.
By November 2020, Apple launched the TSMC-built M1 chip and started dropping Intel from the Mac too.

By July 2025, Apple had sold 3 billion iPhones.

Today Intel is worth $272 billion.
TSMC is worth $1.6 trillion.

What The Chip Happened To AI Stock Investors Today (NEWS EVEN ON THE WEEKEND)!!

SK Hynix
$SKHY
The weekend's wildest headline came from memory. The Information reported Friday night that SoftBank's Masayoshi Son approached Wall Street institutions about financing a buyout of SK Hynix worth roughly $1 trillion. SoftBank didn't deny it, saying only that the idea is "no longer under active consideration," and SK Hynix said it had no knowledge of the matter and that any foreign takeover needs Korean government approval. The deal itself is reported, the statements are confirmed. What it really shows is how strategic HBM has become: Son owns pieces of almost every layer of AI except memory. The open question is whether anyone else starts thinking about memory this way.

Samsung
$SSNLF
Samsung's memory story kept tightening even as chip stocks sold off. Korean outlet Economy Tribune reported Saturday, citing a person familiar with the matter, that most of Samsung's memory capacity through 2029 is already booked, with some customers asking for supply guarantees that stretch into the next decade. That part is a report. What is confirmed comes from Samsung's own Q3 call, where it said long term deals were signed with 10 customers, more are in negotiation, and the contracts carry price floors. Put that next to Micron's sold out comments on Friday and the memory makers are all telling the same story. The caveat is that contracts only matter if customers can keep paying.

TSMC
$TSM
Taiwan stepped in after its market had its worst week in decades. The Taiex fell more than 6% on Friday and about 17.5% for the week, and on Saturday the Financial Supervisory Commission confirmed a blanket ban on short selling below the previous close starting Monday, the first since 2015. It also raised short selling margin requirements, paused new put warrant listings and encouraged buybacks. This is confirmed by the regulator. For AI investors, Taiwan is the supply chain, and TSMC dominates the index, so this is a government trying to stop forced selling in its most important asset. The open question is whether bans calm the market or just delay the selling.

Amazon
$AMZN
Amazon may be about to spend real money on the chip war with Nvidia. The Financial Times reported Saturday that Amazon is in advanced talks to buy AI startup Decart for about $7.5 billion, with a deal possibly announced as early as next week. Decart's software helps AI models run efficiently across different chips, and it was an early showcase customer for Amazon's Trainium. Neither company has confirmed anything, so treat this as a report. If it closes, Amazon is buying a tool that makes moving workloads off Nvidia GPUs easier, which fits the custom silicon theme. The caveat is the price, roughly double the valuation Decart raised at in May.

SpaceX
$SPCX
Elon Musk added a sober note to the AI financing debate. In a post on X Saturday, he wrote that getting this much compute "turned on, cooled and working reliably is incredibly hard," and that "the cash shortage is also going to be nuts next year." His point is that even a few months of delay between paying for compute and earning revenue from it means hundreds of billions of extra working capital across the industry. These are his own words, not a report. It lands right after SpaceX's giant GPU financing, and it echoes the credit worries hitting neoclouds. The open question is who funds that gap if markets stay shut.

posts.text:
Buy when the VIX spikes, not when the headlines clear

A sharp rise in the VIX has repeatedly been followed by solid equity returns. The pattern is clear enough that it is worth revisiting after the latest episode.

On 20 November the VIX jumped 9.29 points to 37.73. The S&P 500 fell 3.43 per cent and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 5.95 per cent. Since the start of 1996 there have been 90 sessions in which the VIX rose by more than five points in a single day. 

In the periods that followed those days, the median forward return for the S&P 500 was 5.62 per cent over three months, 10.86 per cent over six months and 19.87 per cent over one year. The Nasdaq 100 recorded corresponding median gains of 8.40 per cent, 16.66 per cent and 31.14 per cent. Returns are measured from the close on the day of the spike.

The current volatility term structure reinforces the contrary signal. Spot VIX is above the levels priced three and six months ahead, indicating that investors are paying a premium for near-term protection. Fear is concentrated in the present.

A violent sell-off changes quoted prices immediately. It does not erase the customers, competitive positions or cash-generation capacity of sound businesses. The practical implication is selective: quality and diversified equity exposure have historically been the assets that recovered most reliably once the immediate panic subsided.

Markets rarely present attractive entry points under calm headlines. The more common setting is falling prices and elevated demand for protection. The historical record after large daily VIX increases shows that those moments have, on average, rewarded investors who were prepared to act while others were still focused on the risks that had already materialised.

In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

posts.text: More info about Tesla Reality View:

quoted.text:
In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

By Douglas Kass  AUG 21 2008

After acquiring General Re in 1998, Warren Buffett, the veteran investor, learnt the hard way that “derivatives are like hell, easy to enter but almost impossible to exit”.

Four years later, Mr Buffett, chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, argued that highly complex financial instruments and derivatives were time bombs and that these “financial weapons of mass destruction” might harm the econ­omic system. His caution was prescient – like that of many others who have identified company frauds or diagnosed previous credit cycles gone wild.

Yet most of these gloomy messengers have been ignored.

Since Mr Buffett’s warning, financial markets have imploded and policymakers have failed to address the abuses that created the crisis, from the excess leverage of banks to ratings agency failures. Instead, public policy has become focused on a blame game aimed at res­tricting the short-selling of securities – especially of a financial kind.

In July, Christopher Cox, chairman of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, announced a plan to curb improper (naked) short-selling. In doing so he has (de facto) attempted to limit the activity of short-sellers. Mr Cox seems to be implicitly blaming the shorts for the unprecedented fall of bank, ­government-sponsored agency and brokerage stocks over the past year – even though short-sellers were the very group that warned of the dangerous credit cycle and its consequences.

Short-selling runs deep in financial history. Perhaps the first case dates to 1609 when the Dutch trader, Isaac Le Maire, targeted the shares of the shipping company Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie (the Dutch East India Company). VOC was the first multinational corporation in history and had broad powers. Nonetheless, Le Maire, concerned about threats of attack by English ships, sold VOC’s shares short. After learning about Le Maire’s tactics, the stock exchange governing VOC’s trading banned short-selling (although the ban was later revoked). In the early 1630s, the Dutch economy fell into a depression following a speculative peak in the trading of tulips.

Again, short-selling raised the ire of regulators, many of whom saw it as magnifying the effect on the Dutch economic downturn. As a result, England banned short-selling outright. Almost 420 years later – in the late 1920s – short-sellers warned of the consequences of speculation. But in the aftermath of the Wall Street crash of 1929, many blamed them and the uptick rule – which banned short-selling on downticks – was instituted (and stayed in effect until 2007).

More regulation governing short-selling came into force in 1940, with a ban on mutual funds from short-selling (though that law was lifted in 1997). In early 2005, the SEC again sought to restrict the practice. Yet short-sellers have served as financial watchdogs, as many of their warnings have been spot on. The delusional dotcom boom in the late 1990s brought Cassandra-like utterings from the short-selling cabal that proved insightful but were largely ignored.

In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

STOP 🛑 calling this an AI bubble 

In March 2000, at the peak of the dot-com bubble, leading technology stocks traded at extremely high price-to-sales (P/S) ratios. Cisco reached roughly 37x trailing sales, while Microsoft and Oracle traded around 26x. Investors were pricing in years of perfect, uninterrupted growth for internet infrastructure and software companies many of which were not yet highly profitable.

By contrast, in late 2026 the major AI-related stocks are trading at far lower multiples. NVIDIA sits around 8.7x trailing sales (roughly 6.5-7.5x on forward estimates), Microsoft around 10.5× trailing (about 9x forward), and Alphabet near 7× trailing (closer to 5.5-6.5x forward). Even after strong multi-year runs, these companies are valued at a fraction of the 2000 peaks.

The gap is striking because today’s large AI names are already highly profitable, generate substantial cash flow, and have demonstrated real product demand, whereas many 2000 era leaders were still early in monetizing the internet. While elevated AI capital spending introduces some uncertainty, the current multiples show that investors are not pricing these stocks anywhere near the extreme optimism of the 2000 bubble.

Everyone is scratching his head after the recent market sell-off, but it’s really not that complicated. It’s pure math. Let’s take a look, shall we?

At their peaks, the major listed AI-exposed companies (Mag7 plus key chip, foundry, and infrastructure names) were worth roughly $28–32 trillion. Add Anthropic’s post-IPO valuation of about $1.2–1.5 trillion and an expected OpenAI post-IPO figure around $1.5 trillion, and the total sits in the $30–35 trillion range, approaching half the entire US equity market (recently ~$70–72 trillion).

Once a single theme absorbed that much capital, further large gains required either massive new inflows or more money pulled from everything else. At some point neither was available at the necessary scale. Expecting these names to double again from those peaks implied an incremental $30+ trillion of market value. The rest of the US market was only ~$40 trillion; global equity markets, bonds, and private capital held no unused liquidity of that magnitude ready for AI multiples. Leverage, retail flows, and foreign capital were already heavily committed.

The arithmetic simply stopped working. Prices could no longer be justified by any realistic path of further capital absorption. The pullback was the delayed recognition that the liquidity sucked into the trade had nowhere left to come from. It’s really that simple. Seriously, what were people thinking buying these names at multi-trillion valuations? That they would double again in three months?
